persona.role: HR manager at a logistics company

sent_to_model:
There's a thread on the PeopleWorks board (pasted below) where an HR lead called Brenda is about to lose her salary advance scheme to her Finance Manager, and Peter has just told her to shut it down. I disagree with him quite strongly, and we tried the same approach at our company in 2025 and had to reverse it. I'd like to reply to Peter directly but really for Brenda's benefit, since she has her meeting on the 18th. Please make the case properly, with our numbers, especially the 61 calls reception logged and our 40% net-pay cap, and be respectful to Peter. He's not wrong about everything and I don't want it to read like a fight. I've put our figures and the background below. Please don't name the company, I post there under my own name but I'd rather not drag the firm in.

- we're ~340 staff, depots in Embakasi and Changamwe (Mombasa), mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders, warehouse clerks
- closed advances Feb 2025 after Finance pushback. Same argument as Peter almost word for word. gave 2 months notice + one financial literacy session with the SACCO
- in the 6 months after, debt collector / loan app calls to the office went from a handful to 61 logged by reception. Some apps were calling supervisors listed as "referees"
- unplanned absence on the 2 days after month-end rose. Fleet manager linked at least 3 missed Mombasa runs to drivers "sorting out" loans
- reopened Sept 2025 as a written policy - max 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle, repaid in full at next payroll, no fee, request through the payroll portal not my office
- Employment Act limits total deductions to two-thirds of wages, so we check that before approving. Nobody ends up with nothing at month end
- since reopening about 55-70 requests a month, average around KES 9,000. Recovered 100% except 2 leavers, total written off roughly KES 14,000 for the year
- SACCO loans take 2-3 weeks to process and need guarantors. Useless for a child sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday
- loader at Changamwe, 6 apps at once by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to pay the other. Took us 4 months with payroll to unwind it
- our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself because the forecast impact is known in advance - it's a fixed ceiling, not a surprise
- previous scheme: informal; preferred alternative: written rules and limits
- loan-app collection: supervisors contacted as referees; workplace consequences
- financial literacy useful; limited emergency affordability at KES 28,000/month
- compare advance administration/write-offs with absence, missed runs and staff time; latter costs spread across departments
- Brenda goes into the 18th with numbers, not a feeling
- give her the shape of a policy she can propose (cap, frequency, repayment, approval route)
- acknowledge Peter's payroll experience genuinely

Thread: Finance wants to scrap salary advances completely. Am I wrong to push back?
(I'm Wanjiru_K here. I'm replying to Mutua_Peter's message of 2026-11-04T07:58:00.)

---

From: Brenda_Atieno | 2026-11-03T08:42:00
Morning all. I'm HR lead at a mid-size food processing firm in Athi River, about 210 staff, mostly line workers on the lower pay grades. We have always given salary advances informally: someone comes to my office, explains, and if their supervisor agrees we pay them part of their salary early through payroll. No real policy, no limit written anywhere.

Our new Finance Manager wants to stop it entirely from January. His view is that we are not a bank, it messes up the cash flow forecast, and some people are taking an advance literally every month. He has a point on the last one, I won't lie.

My worry is that if we stop, people won't stop needing money. They will just go elsewhere and it will come back to us in other ways. But I can't put numbers on that and he can. Has anyone been through this? Did you scrap advances, keep them, formalise them? I have a meeting with him and the MD on the 18th and I'd like to go in with more than a feeling.

---

From: Kiprono.HRBP | 2026-11-03T10:15:00
We formalised ours two years ago, it was the best compromise. Cap it, put it in writing, make it once a month max. Finance stopped complaining once they could see a ceiling. Can't share our policy doc unfortunately, it's internal, but the bones of it are not complicated.

---

[the message I'm replying to] From: Mutua_Peter | 2026-11-04T07:58:00
I'll be the dissenting voice. I ran payroll for nine years before moving into HR and I'm with your Finance guy. Advances teach people to live on next month's money. You end up with staff who are permanently one month behind and HR becomes the lender of first resort. When someone leaves owing you, good luck recovering it.

There are SACCOs for this. There are banks. Even the mobile loan apps, as bad as they are, are the employee's own decision and their own contract. The company shouldn't be in that business. Every hour you spend approving advances is an hour you're not spending on actual HR work.

My advice: give staff three months' notice, point them to the SACCO, do a financial literacy session, and close the window. It's painful for one or two pay cycles and then people adjust. They always do.

---

From: Brenda_Atieno | 2026-11-04T09:20:00
Thanks both. Peter, that's more or less exactly what Finance will say in the meeting, so it's useful to hear it put so clearly. Anyone who has actually tried closing the window, how did it go?

(About me: HR manager at a logistics company, 40, Nairobi, Kenya. Length: it should come to roughly 800-2,000 words.)

must_cover: Makes the case against closing advances using the closure experience and the 61 logged calls.
Explains the replacement policy including the forty-percent cap, frequency, repayment and approval route.
Compares the policy costs with consequences of closure and limitations of SACCO loans.
Acknowledges Peter’s payroll experience and concerns while giving Brenda evidence for her meeting.
must_not_reveal: The name of the writer’s employer.
